The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Looking at this problem, I need to understand what happens when Mark repeatedly applies the gcd/lcm operation until the board stabilizes.

## Key Observations

**Invariant:** For each prime $p$, the multiset of exponents $\{\nu_p(1), \nu_p(2), \ldots, \nu_p(2100)\}$ is preserved, since $\nu_p(\gcd(a,b)) + \nu_p(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)) = \nu_p(a) + \nu_p(b)$.

**Stable state:** Mark stops when no move changes the board, meaning for any pair $a, b$ on the board, $\{\gcd(a,b), \operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\} = \{a, b\}$. This means one divides the other — the numbers form a **chain under divisibility**: $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_{2100}$.

## Determining the Final State

Since $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_{2100}$, for each prime $p$:
$$\nu_p(d_1) \leq \nu_p(d_2) \leq \cdots \leq \nu_p(d_{2100})$$

So $\nu_p(d_k)$ is the **$k$-th smallest** value in $\{\nu_p(1), \ldots, \nu_p(2100)\}$.

## Computing $\nu_p(d_{2026})$

The value $\nu_p(d_{2026}) = j$ iff exactly $\lfloor 2100/p^j \rfloor \geq 75$ values are $\geq j$ (i.e., at most $2100 - 2026 + 1 = 75$ values can be $\geq j+1$), specifically:

$$\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^j} \right\rfloor \geq 75 \quad \text{and} \quad \left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^{j+1}} \right\rfloor < 75$$

| Prime $p$ | $\lfloor 2100/p \rfloor$ | $\lfloor 2100/p^2 \rfloor$ | $\lfloor 2100/p^3 \rfloor$ | $\lfloor 2100/p^4 \rfloor$ | $\lfloor 2100/p^5 \rfloor$ | $\nu_p(d_{2026})$ |
|-----------|--------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| 2         | 1050                     | 525                       | 262                       | 131                       | 65                        | **4**             |
| 3         | 700                      | 233                       | 77                        | 25                        | —                         | **3**             |
| 5         | 420                      | 84                        | 16                        | —                         | —                         | **2**             |
| 7         | 300                      | 42                        | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 11        | 190                      | 17                        | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 13        | 161                      | 12                        | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 17        | 123                      | 7                         | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 19        | 110                      | 5                         | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 23        | 91                       | 3                         | —                         | —                         | —                         | **1**             |
| 29        | 72 < 75                  | —                         | —                         | —                         | —                         | **0**             |

For all primes $p \geq 29$: $\lfloor 2100/p \rfloor \leq 72 < 75$, so $\nu_p(d_{2026}) = 0$.

## Result

$$d_{2026} = 2^4 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 \cdot 17 \cdot 19 \cdot 23$$

The number of divisors is:
$$(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6 = 5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 64 = 3840$$

$$\boxed{3840}$$
